item.title: Enums
item.description:
A special type that represents a group of constants.Enums in Rust12enum Color{3 Red,4 Blue,5 Yellow,6 Green7}89let treeColor: Color = Color::Green;Rust enums are powerful; each variant can store different types and amounts of data.
1enum Message {2 Quit, // Unit variant, no data3 Move { x: i32, y: i32 }, // Struct variant with named fields4 Write(String), // Tuple variant with one anonymous field5 ChangeColor(i32, i32, i32), // Tuple variant with multiple fields6} Unit variants like Quit store no data. Tuple variants like Write or ChangeColor hold anonymous data. Struct variants like Move have named fields for structured data. About memory allocation The amount of memory rust allocates for a struct is >= largest_size_among_all_fields, when creating the struct it atleast allocates this much. They live on heap as expected. The match expression becomes very powerful when used with enums, since rust checks that all possible values of that enum must be covered in the match statement, below is an example:
1enum Color {2 Red,3 Green,4 Blue,5}67fn main() {8 let color = Color::Red;9 match color {10 Color::Red => println!("Red"),11 Color::Green => println!("Green"),12 Color::Blue => println!("Blue"),13 }14 // you can also access the data inside the enums if they have any15 enum Message {16 Quit, // Unit variant, no data17 Move { x: i32, y: i32 }, // Struct variant with named fields18 Write(String), // Tuple variant with one anonymous field19 ChangeColor(i32, i32, i32), // Tuple variant with multiple fields20 }21 let m = Message::Write;22 match m {23 Message::Write(data_string) => {// name does not matter24 // now this data-string is available here, 25 },26 Message::Move{x, y} => { // name must match27 // notice the different accessor {} instead of ()28 }29 }30 31 // you can also define methods on enums32 // the syntax is same as with structs33 // Match is also possible using specific value contained in the enum34 enum Milk{35 Lowfat(i32),36 Whole37 }38 impl Milk{39 fn drink(self){40 match self {41 Milk::Lowfact(2) => {42 // spefic match that only matches when value = 2 43 } 44 } 45 } 46 }47}Sometimes you want to execute a piece of code for a specific enum value and you don't care about other possible values, sure you can use the match to achieve this, but the you have to match all possible values and even when using - you are writing unreachable code. if let solves that.
if let with enums1enum Milk{2 Lowfat(i32),3 Whole4}5let x: Milk = Milk::Whole;6if let Milk::Whole = x { // syntax is very crucial if let <constant_val> = variable7 // do something8}9// naturally this also will work with all enum variants and the member access if needed works the same as in the match construct10There is also a let else which does the opposite of if let i.e. it only executes when the values are not equal.
let else1let Milk::Whole = x else {2 // do something3}one super confusing difference comes when dealing with non-unit variants, when you do value access with if let then that value is available inside the scope of that if let, in case of let-else the inverse is true, if the else block fails to execute i.e. the condition is true then the member variables declared will be available to the rest of the program outside the let else. But that does not make sense right? How would the compiler know if the dynamic value x matches the conditional? Because if it doesn't know how would it ensure that the parameters declared are available after the block?It requires you to break out of the current scope if you want to run a let else for a method this will be the return.Rust provides a built-in enum called Option to handle cases where a value may or may not be present. It is defined as follows:
1let a = Option::Some(5); // This is a generic enum, the type here is Option<i32>2let b: Option<i32> = Option::None; // there is another way to do this3let b = Option::<i32>::None; // using the turbofish operator Option enum is very useful such is demonstrated by the built in array method get
1let musical_instruments: [i32;3] = [56; 3];23let second = musical_instruments.get(2); // This returns an Option<&String> By default Option implements the copy-trait.
Because Option is so common its members are already in scope use Option::* implicitly, so you can directly do something like Some or None. See The Rust Prelude The "unwrap" method attempts to extract the associated data out of the Some variant. If the variant is None it will result in a RuntimeError.
1let fifth = musical_instruments.get(5); // This is the None Variant2let value = fifth.unwrap();The expect method is almost identical to unwrap but it allows us to customize the error message in case it fails.
1let sixth = musical_instruments.get(6);2let value = sixth.expect("Unable to retrieve element from the array");There is also an unwrap_or method, which can take a default value to return in case the unwrap is called on the None variant.
1let value = fifth.unwrap_or(-1); The match syntax is very useful for Option since it forces you to cover all possible cases unlike unwrap and expect. The Rust Prelude The Rust prelude is a collection of named constructs that are available automatically in every program eg: types, functions, Option etc. Some other constructs require manual importing. A result can be either a Success or an Error.
1pub enum Result<T,E>{2 Ok(T),3 Err(E),4} match operator works very well with it. Like Option, this enum also has very useful impl methods. unwrap: In case of success the data is returned else panics. expect: Works the same way as Option's expect. unwrap_or: Works the same way as Unwrap or. is_ok: Returns boolean is_err

item.title: Macros
Data Types in Rust
item.description:
Data types in Rust are divided into 2 broad categories:These data types only hold 1 value. There are 4 scalar types- integers, Booleans, floating point numbers & characters. These scalar types are subdivided into further types. isize & usize are platform dependent for example for 32 bit architecture. There is no concept of truthy and falsy values in rust, there is only boolean which is either true or false 1int my_variable: u8 = 15;2int my_float = 15.0f32Numerical Representation Like other languages, Rust provides syntax to make numeric values more readable, for example- you can have underscores _ between numbers anywhere and rust will ignore those, 100_000. There is also a scientific notation- let c = 6.02e23; // Avogadro's number-ish (f64) These types store more than 1 value. There are 2 primitive compound types Tuples & Arrays. Fixed size collection of homogenous data.
1let myArray: [f32; 3] = [14.023,15f32,16.2342]; // Array of type f32 and length 32// All elements can be initialized to the same value.3let ys: [i32; 500] = [0; 500];Important information about arrays: Like all other variables, they must be initialized while defining. There are syntactic sugars for initializing such as [0;5] initializes a 5 element array with all elements having value zero. Access is done by index operator like other languages my_array[0] len() method is used to get the length. All data is by default immutable until the array itself is made mutable. Simple, Fixed-Size & Heterogenous collections.
1let person = ("Alice", 30, true); // &str, i32, bool2let employee: (&str, i32, f64) = ("Bob", 45, 3.14);3let single = (5u32,); // Tuple with one element requires a comma to distinguish from plain parenthesisAccessing elements:
1let t = ("hi", 5, 'c');2println!("{}", t.0); // By index3let (greeting, number, ch) = t; // By destructuringUnit Tuple A tuple with no members (), this is the default return type of functions in case it is not specified implicitly or explicitly. These are non-primitive compound types. There are basically three main strings you need to know about. String: From the standard library, mutable objects which store collection of characters, created as String::from("Hello") or "Hello".to_string()
String Literals: Immutable objects stored neither in the Stack or the Heap but baked in the binary, rust uses interning on them. The above examples to create a String use literals as base. They have internal type of &'static str, sometimes also referred to as slices. &str: Immutable reference to a UTF-8 string which is either a literal(the above) or a part of String.
Up Next: Type CastingThis is the juice of how you use strings in rust. This section covers it in more detail.This function is used to append data to the String. String characters are stored as contiguous memory, so if the heap doesn't have enough capacity in that stack pointer location, a new heap memory is found and the address of the pointer is auto updated.
push_str example1let mut name = String::from("Sameer");2name.push_str(" Trivedi");These are applicable for both Arrays and Strings
Slices example1// Heap allocated string 2let my_string = String::from("hello_world");3let my_slice: &str = &my_string[0..3];4let my_string_from_slices = my_slice.to_string();5// String slices always have same type &str, no matter they were derived from a literal or a String6let mut my_string = String::from("hello_world");7let my_mutable_slice = &mut my_string[0..4]; // Does not work with literals though, only slices of Strings are mutable, those also don't have the String methods, making them very limited8let mut my_array = [1,2,3];9let my_array_slice = my_array[0..1]; // has the full array logic, i.e you can modify an index if you want1011// Interesting Observation12 let test = {13 let test = "sims";14 test15 };16 println!("{test}"); // Not out of scope, since &'static str and its slices are baked into the binary there no dangling pointerRange slices are not based on indices The range x..y might seem like it will give slice starting from index x till y. This is mostly true, but the x and y are not indexes, but are byte positions, if the character occupies more than one bytes, then rust will panic at runtime, since slicing those characters is not possible. However for Arrays it is based on index 🙈
Deref Coercion Take a look at the following code: 1fn greet(name: &str) {2 println!("Hello, {}!", name);3}4fn main() {5 let owned_name = String::from("Alice");6 let borrowed_name = "Bob";7 greet(&owned_name); // &String → &str (deref coercion)8 greet(borrowed_name); // &str → &str (no conversion)9 } The function greet takes &str, but accepts both &String and &str arguments thanks to Rust's automatic deref coercion. When you pass &owned_name (which is &String), Rust automatically converts it to &str because String implements Deref<Target = str>.

item.title: Generics
item.description:
Generics let you write type-safe code that works with multiple types using type parameters.Generics Example1fn generic_function<T>(value: T) -> T {2 value;3} During compilation, rustc generates multiple functions based on the variants of T, this behavior is called monomorphization. By default the compiler guesses the most appropriate type for T, but we can force our own types using the turbofish operator.
1generic_function::<i64>(6);Standard stuff
1fn multiple_generics<T, U>(a: T, b: U) -> (T, U) {2 (a, b)3}of course you can mix non generic types with generic ones
1fn mix_generics<T>(a: T, b: i32) -> (T, i32) {2 (a, b)3}You can define structs with generic type parameters.
1struct TreasureChest<T>{2 pirate: String,3 value: double,4 treasure: T5}
1// Setting the type beforehand2impl TreasureChest<String> {3 fn display_treasure(&self) {4 println!("The treasure is: {}", self.treasure);5 }6}7// Generic impl block8impl<T> TreasureChest<T> {9}
1enum Maybe<T> {2 Some(T),3 None,4}

item.title: Control Flow
item.description:
The if statement is weird, look at the syntaxStrange Syntax for if1if expression { // you dont need parenthesis here2 3} // but you need the curly bracesAnd yes you have else and else if like any sane language
else & else if in rust1if expression {2 3}4else if expression2 { // Pardon my .NET psychopath habits5 6}7else {89}Yes due to implicit returns and if-else ladder being technically a block, you can assign values out of it.
Value assignment from if-else1let age = 17;2 let voting_allowed: bool = if age >= 18 { true } else { false }; // This whole line starting from let is an "expression" the if is a "statement" which returns a value but this whole line is an expression.3 println!("{}", voting_allowed);
Read More: Statements vs ExpressionsThey went with "match" like our good old snake_friend 🐍. Below is the syntax-
The Match Statement1let evalution: bool = true;23match evaluation { // no break needed like other languages4 // Patterns/arms5 true => {6 // do something7 }8 false => {9 // do something else10 }11 _ => {// '_' is a variable name, you can have anything else if you are actually using the variable12 // default, I know its a sh^t example13 }14}15// multiple match is also possible using the | operator16// case1 | case 2 | case 3 A good safety feature of rust is that it checks whether all possible paths have been covered before the code can compile in a match statement. And assignment also works like above.
Fallthrough and multi-match By design rust match arms don't have a break statement, so it does not support fallthrough statements like if and if-else. To do a multi-match you follow the below syntax. Even the curly braces are optional, you can just write a single line after => 1match x {21 | 2 => { /* shared logic for 1 and 2 */ },3_ => { /* rest */ }4}
Every match arm must return a value because the RHS of the => is a "statement" and they must be of same type, if it doesn't return anything it returns a Unit Tuple In this episode or Rusty Voodoo we are looking at matched if-else.
match arms with conditionals1match x {2 n if n > 0 => {3 if n % 2 == 0 {4 "positive even"5 } else {6 "positive odd"7 }8 }9 n if n < 0 => {10 if n % 2 == 0 {11 "negative even"12 } else {13 "negative odd"14 }15 }16 0 => "zero",17 _ => "unknown",18}
Read More: Unreachable macro
Up Next: Loops

item.title: Structs
item.description:
A struct or structure is a container for related pieces of data.There are 3 types of structs in rust: Named Type Structs: Fields have names, this is the most common type of struct. Tuple structs: These are like tuples but have a name. Which can be used to create more instances of the struct type. Unit structs: These structs don't have any fields. These are used when you want a type to implement traits but don't want to store any data. 1/* Named Type Structs */2struct Person {3 name: String,4 age: u8 5}67let heroine = Person {8 name: String::from("Daenerys Targaryen"),9 age: 19710}; // Notice the delimiter1112println!("{} was the rightful heir to the Iron Throne", heroine.name);1314/* Tuple structs */15struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);1617let black = Rgb(255,255,255);1819println!("R value of black is: {Rgb.0}");2021/* Unit structs */22struct Marker;2324let m1 = Marker; Mutability of Fields All fields are either mutable or immutable depending on whether the variable that owns the struct is declared as mut
Field Init Shorthand and Spreading Like TS and JS Object property shorthand, rust has a handy syntactical sugar for doing below 1struct Player {2 class: String,3 name: String, 4 level: u85}6
7fn create_player(class: String, name: String, level: u8) -> Player {8 Player {9 class,10 level,11 name 12 } 13} Apart from this it also has spreading, which in Rust is called "struct update syntax": 1fn level_up_player(player: Player) -> Player {2 Player {3 level: player.level + 1,4 ..player // Must be written last in the syntax field and rust will not replace anything that was declared before the spread5 }6}78// Example usage:9let player1 = Player {10 class: String::from("Warrior"),11 name: String::from("Alice"),12 level: 513};1415let player2 = level_up_player(player1);16// player2 will have class: "Warrior", name: "Alice", level: 6 We can define functions on structs, a function can either belong to instance of struct or struct itself (called associated function)
Struct Methods1const PI: f64 = 3.14;2struct Circle {3 radius: f644}56impl Circle {7 fn calc_area(&self: Self) -> f64 { // You can also pass self and mut self which will result in an ownership transfer8 PI * self.radius * self.radius9 }10 fn increase_radius(&mut self: &mut Circle, increase_by: f64) {11 self.radius += increase_by;12 }13 // Associated function (does not take self)14 fn get_sides() -> u8 {15 0 16 }17} A struct can define multiple impl blocks, during compilation it will combine all the blocks to create the final implementation. Every method returns the instance itself. Like in C#
1builder.AddOptions().AddHttpClient().AddControllers();Its also possible in rust:
1#[derive(Clone)]2struct Builder {3 options: Vec<String>,4}56impl Builder {7 fn new() -> Self {8 Self {9 options: Vec::new(),10 }11 }1213 fn add_option(mut self, opt: String) -> Self { // we can also return a mutable reference14 self.options.push(opt);15 self16 }1718 fn build(self) -> Vec<String> {19 self.options20 }2122fn main() {23 let builder = Builder::new()24 .add_option("option1".to_string())25 .add_option("option2".to_string());2627 let result = builder.build();28 println!("{:?}", result);29}

item.title: Ownership
item.description:
Ownership is a set of compile-time rules that the compiler checks for to ensure the program will be free of memory errors.Owner is something that is responsible for cleaning up a piece of memory when it is no longer in use. Every value in a rust program has a 1 owner. The owner can change over the course of a program.Move this refers to transfer of ownership from one owner to another in rust.Ownership Transfer1let name = String::from("Sameer"); // lives in heap, name stores the **pointer**2let next = name; // Ownership transferred, now next is the ONLY pointer pointin to the String3println!("{name}"); // name is useless now, this won't compile.Rust's Borrowing RulesRust allows multiple ways to access data, but with strict safety rules:Immutable References (&T) You can create multiple immutable references to the same data These references only allow reading the data, not modifying it Multiple immutable references can coexist safely since no one can change the data Mutable References (&mut T) Only one active mutable reference can exist at a time This reference allows both reading and modifying the data No other references (mutable or immutable) can exist while a mutable reference is active The Key Rule: Exclusive Access At any given time, you can have either: Multiple immutable references, OR Exactly one active mutable reference A reference is considered "active" from when it's created until its last use, not just until the end of its scope. Below is an example:
1let mut data = vec![1, 2, 3];2let immut_ref = &data; // immutable reference created3println!("{:?}", immut_ref); // last use of immutable reference4let mut_ref = &mut data; // mutable reference created (OK!)5mut_ref.push(4); // use mutable reference Immutable references implement the copy trait.
The drop function drop(&mut self) function is a special function which is called by Rust at the end of a scope which cleans up the data in the heap or signals the rust runtime to do so. This only works on heap allocated memory. You can also define the drop function which is a part of the Drop trait, for custom types. Also it can be manually called whenever you want for the types that implement it, this makes them unusable. 1let mut person = String::from("Test");2drop(person);3println!("{person}");
1fn consume_string(s: String) { // This can also be mut s: String even if the previous owner is not mutable2 println!("{}", s);3 // s is dropped here4}56let my_string = String::from("hello");7consume_string(my_string); // my_string is moved, no longer accessible
1fn read_string(s: &String) {2 println!("{}", s);3}45let my_string = String::from("hello");6read_string(&my_string); // my_string is still accessible after the call
1fn modify_string(s: &mut String) {2 s.push_str(" world");3}45let mut my_string = String::from("hello");6modify_string(&mut my_string);7println!("{}", my_string); // prints "hello world"
1fn process_str(s: &str) { // Immutable reference2 println!("{}", s);3}45// Works with both String and &str6let owned = String::from("hello");7let borrowed = "world";8process_str(&owned);9process_str(borrowed);
When functions return a variable, there is again an ownership transfer, following the same set of rules. The function is no longer responsible for drop.
Compound types such as Arrays & Tuples, own each element inside them. So when their elements are accessed, a full copy needs to be created or access must be done via reference.
Arrays & Tuples Ownership1let my_array = [1,2,3];2let el = my_array[0]; // Full copy created, only possible when copy trait implemented by type3let my_array_2 = [String::from("Test")]4let el_2 = my_array_2[0] // Throws error, either .clone() must be used or el_2 must hold a reference.

item.title: Reference & Borrowing
item.description:
Borrowing means taking something without transferring ownership, a borrower must return the reference. Borrowing involves creating a reference to a value. Generally Heap Data's reference are used, but stack data can also be referenced. Reference example1let my_val: i32 = 2;2let my_ref: &i32 = &my_val; // Type address leading to i32References must never outlive their referent.
Dereference example1println!("{*my_ref}");Rust auto dereferences display trait implementing types

item.title: Traits
item.description:
A trait is a contract that requires the types that implement the trait to have certain functionality according to the contract. Imagine them like an interface in C# and Java and abstract classes in C++. They enable polymorphism in Rust.Following are some useful built in traits.Mandates a format method on the type which can output string representation, used while printing the data using println!.1println!("This is my integer {}", 32);Debug should format the data to a programmer facing string which is useful for debugging.
1#[derive(Debug)] // easy shortcut to auto add debug trait to types2struct Point {3 x: i32,4 y: i32,5}67fn main() {8 let p = Point { x: 3, y: 7 };9 println!("{:?}", p); // Output: Point { x: 3, y: 7 }10 println!("{:#?}", p); // Pretty-printed11}Mandates that the type can be copied (Full duplicate). This forces the compiler to treat operations such as assignment, passing arg as value as NOT MOVE. Basically something that can be copied using memcpy.
Copy Trait Example1let x = 24;2let y = x; // 2 separate copies34#[derive(Copy, Clone)] // For custom types both copy and clone must be derived5struct Point {6 x: i32, // All fields of the type must implement Copy on their own7 y: i32,8}Copy Behavior for Heap Allocated Types Heap allocated types such as Vec<T> do not implement the copy trait. Such data types when assigned to another variable a duplicate reference pointing to the same data on the heap is created. Any type can implement this trait unlike copy. This introduces a special method .clone() on the object. This is where you implement complex logic to do clone the whole objects.Copy and Clone are closely related Copy is essentially derived from clone i.e its a subset. Copy types must implement Clone because Copy is essentially saying "my clone() operation is so cheap it can happen implicitly.

item.title: Stack and Heap
item.description: Yes these are the same ones you studied in Operating Systems class. Stack and Heap are 2 memory regions where data is stored during program execution. Good old stack, below is the diagram which tells you "where" this stack isProcessMemoryStaticHeapCodeThreadRegistersStackThreadRegistersStackThreadRegistersStackLike any other stack, this is also a LIFO structure. Very fast for allocation and deallocation.In Rust stack is used for storing: Scalar types (integers, booleans, characters) Fixed size arrays Structs and enums where all fields have known sizes Function parameters etc. The location of heap is also mentioned in the above drawing. This is used for data which is unknown or has variable type at compile time. Allocation is slower than the stack and pointers are required for data access.Rust stores the following in heap: Data types with dynamic or unknown size, such as Vec<T> Large data, only pointer to the data resides on the stack. If data needs to outlive the function or scope where it was created, heap allocation is often necessary. Box pointer 📦 All values in Rust are stack allocated by default. Values can be boxed (allocated on the heap) by creating a Box<T>. A box is a smart pointer to a heap allocated value of type T. When a box goes out of scope, its destructor is called, the inner object is destroyed, and the memory on the heap is freed. Memory safety without a Garbage Collector? Rust claims to be memory safe, but it does not have a garbage collector. Well there are a lot of tricks in the crabs claws, one of them is automatically calling the destructor of an allocated value once it goes out of scope. See also: Copy trait

item.title: Loops
item.description:
⚠️ Another because I said so syntax ahead-The loop keyword1loop {2 println!("Infinite loop");3}In the loop keyword you have to manually break out of the loop using break statement when you are done. There is also a continue statement.
1fn main() {2 for i in 1..10 {3 if i == 3 {4 continue;5 }6 if i == 7 {7 break;8 }9 println!("{}", i);10 }11} The loop loop can return a value as well, this is done using the break statement break value_to_return; This only works in the loop loop Standard while loop nothing special.
While loop1let mut i = 0;2while i < 15 {3 i += 1;4 println!("{i}");5} Break and continue work the same way but unlike loop loop, it cannot return via break. The good ol' for-loop
All for loop uses1fn main() {2 // 1. Basic for loop over a range (exclusive end)3 println!("Basic range (1..6):");4 for i in 1..6 {5 println!(" {}", i); // Prints 1 to 56 }78 // 2. Inclusive range (includes the end)9 println!(" Inclusive range (1..=6):");10 for i in 1..=6 {11 println!(" {}", i); // Prints 1 to 612 }1314 // 3. Iterating over an array15 let fruits = ["Apple", "Orange", "Banana"];16 println!(" Array iteration:");17 for fruit in fruits {18 println!(" {}", fruit); // Prints each fruit19 }2021 // 4. Index-based iteration over an array22 let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];23 println!(" Index-based iteration:");24 for i in 0..colors.len() {25 println!(" The color name is {}", colors[i]); // Uses index to access element26 }2728 // 5. Using enumerate to get (index, value) pairs29 let items = ["x", "y", "z"];30 println!(" Enumerate for index and value:");31 for (index, value) in items.iter().enumerate() {32 println!(" {}: {}", index, value); // Prints index and value33 }3435 // 6. Reverse iteration (descending order)36 println!(" Range reversed (1..6).rev():");37 for i in (1..6).rev() {38 println!(" {}", i); // Prints 5 to 139 }4041 // 7. Stepping by intervals (e.g., every 2nd number)42 println!(" Range with step_by(2) (0..10).step_by(2):");43 for i in (0..10).step_by(2) {44 println!(" {}", i); // Prints 0, 2, 4, 6, 845 }46}
Read More: Recursions

item.title: Functions
item.description:
I am not going to define functions, that would be absurd. Below is the syntax however if I ever get dementia. Rust is a functional programming language so you have pretty much all function functionalities with added extras.Parameters vs Arguments Functions may declare a set of input variables as parameters, through which the caller passes arguments into the function Sample Function1fn my_function(){2 // Body here3}Well there are a few differences between the functions you see in other languages-You don't have to add an explicit return statement for functions.
Implicit Return Example1fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 { // The return type is a must when your function returns anything other than a unit tuple 2 x + y // implicit return (no semicolon)3}45// This behaviour is not limited to functions, any block's last statement is an implicit return6let x = {7 let k = 2.14;8 k*k9}Notice the semi-colon (Statements vs Expressions) Statements in rust end with a semi-colon and do not return a value, Expressions don't end with a semi-colon and do return a value, in the implicit return the last line has to be an expression for it to work. Furthermore if you specified a return type in the function definition and then add a statement at the end of the function, it will trigger a compile time error. Parameters can take ownership, borrow immutably, or borrow mutably:
Ownership Example1fn take_ownership(s: String) { /* s is moved here */ }2fn borrow_immutably(s: &String) { /* s is borrowed */ }3fn borrow_mutably(s: &mut String) { /* s is mutably borrowed */ } The default return type for a function without any explicit or implicit returns i.e. void is a Unit Tuple

item.title: Constants in Rust
item.description: For a constant in rust the following hold true: Its value never changes. It must be declared and initialized at the same time means the value must be known at compile time. Cannot be shadowed Can live in a global scope unlike Variables. 1const MY_CONSTANT = 24.5;

item.title: Generics in Rust
item.description: Generics are abstract stand-ins for concrete types. You define them using angle brackets <>Declare basic generic types1struct Point<T> {2 x: T,3 y: T,4}56let integer = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };7let float = Point { x: 1.1, y: 2.2 };

item.title: Ranges
Operators
item.description: Rust supports all common operators, and they are not batshit crazy to floor towards negative infinity for negative divisions. And there is no crazy things like == & ===. There is no ++ and -- cause who needs that but all compoud assignment operators are there +=, |= and all that.

item.title: Type Casting
item.description: Rust supports type casting with the as keyword. As long as its a plausible conversion.

item.title: IO
item.description:
The println! macro supports interpolation using curly braces,1var my_age = 24;2var my_name = "Sameer";3println!("My age is {}", my_age); // outputs My age is 244println!("My age is {my_age}"); // works the same way how cool is that5println!("My age is {0} & My Name is {1}, My Name was always {1}, I turned {my_age} last year", my_age, myname); // positional arguments start from 0 and can be reused in the target stringprintln! macro provides an option of format specifiers which control how certain data will be printed. Works with all interpolations, just follow with the specifier.Examples
1let name = "Alice";2let age = 30;3println!("{} is {} years old.", name, age);45println!("{:>5}", 42); // right-align6println!("{:<5}", 42); // left-align7println!("{:^7}", 42); // center-align89println!("{:08.2}", 3.1415); // total 8 chars incl decimal = pad + float precision → 00003.141011println!("{name} likes {lang}", name = "Bob", lang = "Rust");1213let arr = [1, 2, 3];14println!("{:?}", arr); // Debug print15There are a lot of these specifiers

item.title: Methods
item.description:
Methods are functions that are defined on types Below is an example on an integer and an &str.1let my_var: i32 = -15;2println!("The absolute value is: {}", my_var.abs()); // built-in method that returns the modulus of the integer.3let s = "hello";4println!("{}", s.len()); // method on &strMethods can't be called on inferred type variables. You must explicitly mention the type of the variable using : to be able to call methods, otherwise rust throws an ambiguous type error and program fails to compile. We can define custom methods on types, but only the types we create. It does not work on built in types.
1struct Circle {2 radius: f64,3}45impl Circle {6 // Method: takes self by reference7 fn area(&self) -> f64 {8 3.1415 * self.radius * self.radius // don't use magic numbers kids 🔫9 }1011 // Associated function: doesn't take self like Static12 fn new(radius: f64) -> Self {13 Circle { radius }14 }15}1617fn main() {18 let c = Circle::new(5.0); // associated function (like a constructor)19 println!("Area: {}", c.area()); // method call on instance20}

item.title: Variables and Mutability
item.description:
Below is how you declare a variable in rust1let my_var = 50; // compiler auto deduces type 'i32' in this caseRust variables are immutable by default, meaning once assigned they cannot be re-assigned.
1my_var = 90; // will throw and error during compilation2let mut myMutableVar = 50; // This defines a mutable variable which CAN be re-assignedRust supports shadowing (surprise, surprise!), meaning a variable can be redeclared in the same scope and the earlier declaration is invalidated (only occurs when done in the same scope).
1let my_var = 50; // i32 as of now2let my_var = "text"; // &str now3// mut or non mut does not matterThe Crab Hates Global Variables So much so that variable declarations can only be done inside a local scope.
Related: Naming Conventions, Data Types in Rust

item.title: Creating a Rust Project
item.description:
The standard way to do this is using cargo.1cargo new project_nameThis command: Creates a folder named hello_world Auto initializes a git repository inside that folder Creates an src subfolder with a main.rs file. Creates a Cargo.toml file for library and version info. The content of main.rs looks like:1fn main() {2 println!("Hello, world!");3}
This command actually creates a so-called binary crate. See Crates in RustThere are a couple of ways of doing this:1rustc main.rsThis produces an executable that then can be run normally.The standard way to go for projects1cargo build # builds and produces a binary which needs to be separately executed2cargo run # build and run in single step3cargo check # checks the program whether it can be compiled, usually faster but IDEs do this job most of the time4cargo clean # removes all old compiled objects and binaries
Build Flags By default the cargo commands do a debug build of the program, which is bulky non optimized version useful for debugging and sifting through instructions. The build and run command accept a build flag which can be used to change the target executable cargo build --release. There are several other build flags in rust, can be found here Built in Autoformatting rustfmt file_name can be used to auto format a rust file, cargo fmt does the same thing for the whole project.

item.title: Crates in Rust
item.description:
A crate is a unit of compilation in rust, simply put it can be called as a package of rust code.There are two types of crates in rust: Binary Crates: Crates that contain executable code. They contain a single main.rs with a main() method. Library Crates: Crates that don't contain executable code and are used to ship reusable code by linking them to other crates. Does not have a main method. Dual Crates? A crate can ship as both a binary and a library crate. In such cases the add command links the library portion of the crate, whereas the install command installs the executable. Like nuget & npm there is a central repository for rust crates. Below are some useful commands -1cargo add crate_name # adds the dependency of the crate_name in current package, ONLY works with library crates2cargo install crate_name # installs the executable globally on your machine crates.io: A Cautionary Tale Cargo install, installs rust crates globally on your machine, although the rust crates are audited but there has been multiple incidents of fake crates. Better be safe with this command. Also there was some Rust Drama where some popular package maintainers self deprecated their packages over a fight.
See Also: Modules in Rust
